30:
- A compiler graph describes operations and their dependencies. One graph can lower to several GPU kernels.
- A CUDA Graph describes GPU execution work that can be captured and replayed. It can contain several kernels and other CUDA operations.
- So one compiler graph doesn’t mean one kernel, and CUDA Graph replay doesn’t mean kernel fusion.
31:
- A tensor is an array of numbers. It doesn’t have to live on a GPU.
- A kernel is a program launched on the GPU. One model layer can involve multiple kernels.
- An intermediate representation, or IR, is the compiler’s structured description of operations and relationships.
- Lowering moves that representation toward executable target instructions.
- A guard checks whether assumptions for a saved plan hold.
- A graph break leaves some behavior outside a captured graph and can split compilation into regions.
11:
- The fused program divides the tensor into blocks of work and calculates the positions it will access.
- It loads input values, performs addition and ReLU locally, then stores the final output values.
- At the edge of an array, a mask prevents access to positions outside the valid range.
- The intermediate value can be held locally rather than written as a separate tensor.
- Combining more operations can increase register use and sometimes hurt performance. Fusion needs compatible dependencies and resource requirements.
15:
- An output tile is a block of results assigned to one program. Its block dimensions determine how much work that program owns.
- Strides describe how far apart neighboring array entries are in memory. The program uses them to locate the needed input blocks.
- It loads input blocks, combines their contributions into partial sums and repeats across the reduction dimension.
- Masks handle positions near the boundaries. After the final contribution, the program stores its completed output block.
- Larger tiles can improve reuse but consume more registers or shared memory. Fewer independent programs may then fit at once.
- A compiler can use heuristics, select an optimized library or benchmark candidate schedules through autotuning.
22:
- A general compiler needs transformations that are valid across a supported set of programs and inputs.
- A workload expert may know an additional fact, such as a fixed graph topology or a sparsity pattern that never changes.
- A specialized implementation can sometimes use that fact to skip work a general implementation must retain.
- That implementation is correct only within its stated input domain, and specialization doesn’t guarantee a speedup.
- Expose supported invariants or use an appropriate specialized operator. Removing guards without preserving their assumptions can make execution incorrect.
25:
- A graph break splits compilation around behavior that wasn’t captured. It can limit optimization across that boundary.
- A recompile means another compiled variant was built. Changing assumptions can cause it, but not every changed input requires a new variant.
- The logging setting on this slide reports graph breaks and recompilations. Set it before starting the Python process.
- The fullgraph option asks for capture as one graph and raises when a graph break prevents it. It doesn’t promise one kernel.
- The dynamic option attempts broader shape handling. It doesn’t remove every constraint or guard.
- The reduce-overhead mode can use CUDA Graphs for eligible workloads. The max-autotune mode spends more preparation time selecting implementations. Support depends on the backend and platform.
24:
- This request gives a coding agent a specific experiment and a fixed correctness boundary.
- We ask it to profile first so it can identify repeated computation that matters to the workload.
- We keep an eager reference, preserve precision and compare correctness before accepting a speed claim.
- Startup cost, warmed latency and memory should be reported separately across representative shapes.
- If results disappoint, the agent can inspect graph-break and recompile logs. Its report should state the environment and timing boundary.
- Changing quantization, precision or model architecture is a separate experiment with its own evaluation.
27:
- Start with the introductory torch.compile tutorial and compare eager with compiled execution on an existing model.
- Then investigate one graph break and one recompilation. That connects the tools to the reuse assumptions we discussed.
- If you want to understand kernels, work through Triton vector addition before matrix multiplication.
- You don’t need to write kernels to benefit from compilation.
- For more depth, the PyTorch compiler paper explains capture and lowering. The CUDA programming guidance explains hardware resource constraints, and CUDA Graph Trees explains replay and memory interactions.
